title: How to Structure a Multi-Region Store Without Splitting Your SEO
excerpt: Selling into two or three countries does not require three separate sites. This guide covers subfolder structure, currency handling and hreflang decisions that keep your authority in one place.
body: The default move when a store starts selling into a second country is to buy another domain and build a second site. It feels tidy, and it quietly halves the value of every piece of content you have already earned. Links, authority and crawl budget are all split across two properties that then compete for the same queries. Unless you have a legal reason to separate, one domain with clear regional subfolders will outperform two domains almost every time, and it is far cheaper to maintain.

Use subfolders rather than subdomains or separate domains. A structure with a market folder per region keeps every page inside the same crawlable property, lets you compare performance in one report, and lets a strong page in one market pass value to its sibling in another. Keep the folder names stable and readable, avoid putting language and country into the same folder unless you genuinely sell both, and never change the structure later without a redirect plan, because regional migrations lose traffic faster than any other kind.

Currency is a separate decision from market, and mixing them causes most of the problems. A customer in one country may want to see prices in a currency that is not theirs, so let the currency switch be a manual control rather than something forced by the visitor's address. Round prices per currency instead of converting them mechanically, because a mechanically converted price looks careless and converts worse. Keep one canonical product record underneath so you are not maintaining two inventories that drift apart over a season.

The DTCwise Store Builders category at /category/storebuilder keeps the current shortlist of platforms with ratings and pricing, which is the fastest way to sanity check whether your current stack already supports regional folders. Do not redirect visitors automatically based on their address. Automatic redirects block crawlers, trap customers who travel, and make it impossible to share a link that works everywhere. Instead, show a dismissible regional prompt and remember the choice. Whatever you do, make sure the same product is reachable at a stable address in every market folder, and that the market folders do not serve identical shipping and returns copy where the actual terms genuinely differ.

Handle the duplicate content question honestly. Regional pages that differ only in currency are near duplicates, and search engines will pick one to show. Make each market page earn its place with local specifics: delivery times from the warehouse that actually serves it, returns address, duties and tax treatment, and payment methods people in that market use. That is real differentiation rather than a swapped word list, and it also reduces the refund rate from customers surprised by duties at the door.

Add reciprocal hreflang tags once the structure is live. Each regional version should reference itself and every other version, including a sensible default for visitors outside your listed markets, and the tags must match the canonical tags rather than contradict them. Validate them in Search Console and check that each market folder is indexed separately. The WooCommerce listing at /tool/woocommerce shows current pricing and the multi currency features worth checking when you plan this structure.
